claim: Traveling waves play an essential role in coordinating mitosis over large distances.
source: Traveling waves play an essential role in coordinating mitosis over large distances, but what determines the spatial origin of mitotic waves remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise for the study.

claim: Nuclei define pacemakers by concentrating cell cycle regulators in cell-free extracts of Xenopus laevis eggs.
source: In cell-free extracts of Xenopus laevis eggs, we find that nuclei define such pacemakers by concentrating cell cycle regulators.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Nuclear positioning determines the pacemaker location in computational models of diffusively coupled oscillators that account for nuclear import.
source: In computational models of diffusively coupled oscillators that account for nuclear import, nuclear positioning determines the pacemaker location.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: The spatial dimensions of the oscillatory medium change the nuclear positioning and strongly influence whether a pacemaker is more likely to be at a boundary or an internal region.
source: Furthermore, we find that the spatial dimensions of the oscillatory medium change the nuclear positioning and strongly influence whether a pacemaker is more likely to be at a boundary or an internal region.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through both modeling and experiments.

claim: Increasing the system width increases the proportion of pacemakers at the boundary.
source: Finally, we confirm experimentally that increasing the system width increases the proportion of pacemakers at the boundary.
evidence: This is an experimental finding confirmed in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 5.

claim: Action potentials propagate along the axon of a neuron.
source: For example, action potentials are well known to propagate along the axon of a neuron (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952), but a wealth of other biological processes have been shown to be coordinated via traveling waves (Winfree, 1987; Dawson et al., 1999; Loose et al., 2008; Chang and Ferrell, 2013; Deneke et al., 2016; Prindle et al., 2015; Bement et al., 2015; Fukujin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952.

claim: Cell cycle oscillations self-organize via mitotic waves in a spatially extended system.
source: In particular, cell cycle oscillations also self-organize via mitotic waves in a spatially extended system (Chang and Ferrell, 2013; Deneke et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chang and Ferrell, 2013 and Deneke et al., 2016.

claim: Mitotic waves coordinate cell division in space in large developing eggs ranging from ≈100 µm to ≈1 mm in diameter that are laid externally by insects, amphibians, and fish.
source: Such waves that coordinate cell division in space are especially relevant in the large developing eggs (ranging from ≈100 µm to ≈1 mm in diameter) that are laid externally by insects, amphibians, and fish, because they are too large to be synchronized by diffusion alone (see Box 1).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the biological context.

claim: Large developing eggs are too large to be synchronized by diffusion alone.
source: Such waves that coordinate cell division in space are especially relevant in the large developing eggs (ranging from ≈100 µm to ≈1 mm in diameter) that are laid externally by insects, amphibians, and fish, because they are too large to be synchronized by diffusion alone (see Box 1).
evidence: This is stated as a reason for the importance of mitotic waves in large eggs.

claim: Cell-free extracts made from eggs of Xenopus laevis exhibit biochemical cell cycle oscillations in vitro that are similar to those found in vivo.
source: Here, we address this open question using cell-free extracts made from eggs of the frog Xenopus laevis, which exhibit biochemical cell cycle oscillations in vitro that are similar to those found in vivo (Murray, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Murray, 1991.

claim: Mitotic waves originate at nuclei, which act as pacemakers.
source: We find that mitotic waves originate at nuclei, which act as so-called pacemakers, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings (Kuramoto, 1984).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Previous studies have suggested centrosomes or nuclei to serve as pacemakers.
source: While previous studies have suggested centrosomes or nuclei to serve as pacemakers (Chang and Ferrell, 2013; Ishihara et al., 2014), their role in organizing mitotic waves has not been empirically demonstrated.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chang and Ferrell, 2013 and Ishihara et al., 2014.

claim: The role of centrosomes or nuclei in organizing mitotic waves has not been empirically demonstrated prior to this study.
source: While previous studies have suggested centrosomes or nuclei to serve as pacemakers (Chang and Ferrell, 2013; Ishihara et al., 2014), their role in organizing mitotic waves has not been empirically demonstrated.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Nuclei serve as pacemakers both in the absence and presence of centrosomes.
source: We provide evidence that nuclei serve as pacemakers, both in the absence and presence of centrosomes.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Having the nucleus setting the pace of the cell cycle may help ensure proper DNA replication prior to initiation of mitosis.
source: Having the nucleus setting the pace of the cell cycle may help ensure proper DNA replication prior to initiation of mitosis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: If the pacemaker were elsewhere, the decision to divide might be decoupled from DNA replication, leading to division occurring before DNA replication completes.
source: If the pacemaker were elsewhere, the decision to divide might be decoupled from DNA replication, leading to division occurring before DNA replication completes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential consequences if the pacemaker were not at the nucleus.

claim: Nuclei can concentrate cell cycle regulators, leading to faster cell cycle oscillations at those nuclear locations.
source: We postulate that nuclei can concentrate cell cycle regulators, leading to faster cell cycle oscillations at those nuclear locations.
evidence: This is a postulate that is tested and supported by the experimental and modeling data.

claim: Nuclei and their spatial positioning, which is affected by the spatial dimensions of the system, determine how the cell cycle is coordinated in space and time.
source: Nuclei and their spatial positioning, which is affected by the spatial dimensions of the system, determine how the cell cycle is coordinated in space and time.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings of the study.

claim: Pacemakers are often located near nuclei that are brighter due to increased import of exogeneously added GFP-NLS.
source: By monitoring mitotic waves in Teflon tubes using time-lapse microscopy (see Box 2), we find that pacemakers are often located near nuclei that are brighter due to increased import of exogeneously added GFP-NLS.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by microscopy data.

claim: The generation of pacemakers does not require centrosomes.
source: We show that the generation of such pacemakers does not require centrosomes and explore the influence of nuclear density and nuclear import strength on cell cycle period and pacemaker wave formation.
evidence: This is an experimental finding demonstrated by using purified DNA without centrosomes.

claim: The distribution of regulators depends on the nuclear positioning and spatial dimensions of the system, with thicker tubes having a larger tendency to concentrate cell cycle regulators at the boundaries.
source: Our modeling shows that the distribution of regulators depends on the nuclear positioning and spatial dimensions of the system, with thicker tubes having a larger tendency to concentrate cell cycle regulators at the boundaries (i.e. outer edges of the tube).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claim: Mitotic waves can originate from the system interior or from the system boundary, depending on the spatial dimensions of the system.
source: Using both numerical simulations and experiments, we go on to show that mitotic waves can originate from the system interior or from the system boundary, depending on the spatial dimensions of the system.
evidence: This is demonstrated through both computational modeling and experiments.

claim: The observed dynamics are the result of competition between waves originating from different pacemaker regions, where the relative strength of the pacemakers in the interior and at the boundary is determined by the system dimensions.
source: These observed dynamics are the result of competition between waves originating from different pacemaker regions, where the relative strength of the pacemakers in the interior and at the boundary is determined by the system dimensions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The mitotic wave at cell cycle 5–6 propagated with a speed of ∼ 20 µm/min.
source: The wave at cell cycle 5–6 was found to propagate with a speed of ∼ 20 µm/min.
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Approximately 250 nuclei/µl are added in the experiment shown in Figure 1A.
source: Approx. 250 nuclei/µl are added.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1A.

claim: The pacemaker location is indicated by the region with the highest GFP-NLS intensity.
source: Left: GFP-NLS intensity profile, averaged over the times between the mitotic waves in cell cycle 5 and 6. The GFP-NLS intensity is highest close to the pacemaker region P.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B analysis panel.

claim: The pacemaker region oscillates fastest.
source: Middle: Difference in cell cycle period (with respect to the fastest period) at different locations along the tube, averaged over cell cycle 1–6, showing that the pacemaker region oscillates fastest.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B analysis panel.

claim: The nucleus close to the pacemaker region P is most separated from its neighbors.
source: Right: Mean distance from the center of each nucleus to its two nearest neighboring nuclei. The nucleus close to the pacemaker region P is most separated from its neighbors.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B analysis panel.

claim: Mitotic waves are observed using a fluorescent microtubule reporter (HiLyte Fluor 488) in a 200 µm Teflon tube.
source: (C) Mitotic waves in a 200 µm Teflon tube shown by a fluorescent microtubule reporter (HiLyte Fluor 488).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Extracts with less added sperm nuclei had a faster cell cycle.
source: We found that extracts with less added sperm nuclei had a faster cell cycle (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The wave speeds were initially faster in extracts with lower nuclear density than in tubes with a higher concentration of sperm nuclei.
source: Mitotic waves were similarly observed, but the wave speeds were initially faster than in tubes with a higher nuclear density (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The waves slowed down to similar speeds as in the case with the higher concentration of sperm nuclei.
source: The waves then slowed down to similar speeds as in the case with the higher concentration of sperm nuclei.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the data in Figure 2A.

claim: The average cell cycle period increases over time for both nuclear densities.
source: For both nuclear densities we also found that the average cell cycle period increases over time (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The correlation of mitotic wave speed with cell cycle duration is consistent with a transition from sweep waves to trigger waves as the cell cycle slows down.
source: Such a correlation of mitotic wave speed with cell cycle duration is consistent with a transition from sweep waves to trigger waves as the cell cycle slows down (Vergassola et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation to Vergassola et al., 2018.

claim: An increase in cell cycle period has been linked to a decrease in ATP supply over time.
source: An increase in cell cycle period has been linked to a decrease in ATP supply over time (Guan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guan et al., 2018.

claim: An increase in cell cycle period could be related to increasing levels of DNA as it is replicated.
source: An additional explanation could be that an increase in cell cycle period is related to increasing levels of DNA as it is replicated (Dasso and Newport, 1990).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to Dasso and Newport, 1990.

claim: A decrease in nuclear density did not lead to a big change in the internuclear distance.
source: Interestingly, a decrease in nuclear density did not lead to a big change in the internuclear distance (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2I.

claim: Decreasing nuclear density created more and larger regions where nuclei were absent.
source: Instead, it created more and larger regions where nuclei were absent (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and pacemakers were predominantly found close to these regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Pacemakers were predominantly found close to regions where nuclei were absent.
source: Instead, it created more and larger regions where nuclei were absent (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and pacemakers were predominantly found close to these regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cheng and Ferrell observed a similar transition from a regular pattern of equidistantly spaced nuclei to a system with holes in Xenopus interphase egg extracts when decreasing the concentration of added sperm nuclei.
source: Cheng and Ferrell observed a similar transition from a regular pattern of equidistantly spaced nuclei to a system with holes in Xenopus interphase egg extracts when decreasing the concentration of added sperm nuclei (Cheng and Ferrell, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cheng and Ferrell, 2019.

claim: Mitotic waves originate at the few nuclei present in the tube when nuclear density is approximately 30 nuclei/µl.
source: Mitotic waves were found to originate at the few nuclei present in the tube, and they traveled through the whole tube (several mm) at a speed of approx. 60 µm/min (Video 1, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Video 1 and Figure 2C.

claim: Mitotic waves traveled through the whole tube at a speed of approximately 60 µm/min when nuclear density is approximately 30 nuclei/µl.
source: Mitotic waves were found to originate at the few nuclei present in the tube, and they traveled through the whole tube (several mm) at a speed of approx. 60 µm/min (Video 1, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Video 1 and Figure 2C.

claim: In the absence of any nuclei in the tube, cell cycle oscillations were observed with periods similar to extracts with low concentrations of demembranated sperm nuclei.
source: In the absence of any nuclei in the tube (no added demembranated sperm nuclei), we still observed cell cycle oscillations with periods similar to extracts with low concentrations of demembranated sperm nuclei (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No mitotic waves were observed in the absence of any nuclei in the tube.
source: However, no mitotic waves were observed (Video 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Video 1.

claim: Centrosomes have been suggested to serve as pacemakers, potentially by concentrating pro-mitotic factors such as Cdc25 and cyclin B.
source: Centrosomes have also been suggested to serve as pacemakers (Chang and Ferrell, 2013; Ishihara et al., 2014), potentially by concentrating pro-mitotic factors such as Cdc25 and cyclin B (Bonnet et al., 2008; Jackman et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chang and Ferrell, 2013; Ishihara et al., 2014; Bonnet et al., 2008; and Jackman et al., 2003.

claim: Demembranated sperm nuclei have associated centrioles, which give rise to centrosomes that can generate microtubule asters.
source: Demembranated sperm nuclei are known to have associated centrioles, which give rise to centrosomes that can generate microtubule asters.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: DNA alone is sufficient to create pacemaker-generated mitotic waves without a need for centrosomes.
source: Mitotic waves were still observed indicating that DNA alone is sufficient to create pacemaker-generated mitotic waves without a need for centrosomes (Figure 2D, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—video 1.

claim: Increasing levels of importazole increase the cell cycle period.
source: Increasing levels of importazole were found to increase the cell cycle period and slowed down the formation of nuclei (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Increasing levels of importazole slow down the formation of nuclei.
source: Increasing levels of importazole were found to increase the cell cycle period and slowed down the formation of nuclei (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Mitotic waves were still observed with similar speeds for lower concentrations of importazole.
source: Mitotic waves were still observed with similar speeds for lower concentrations of importazole, while concentrations higher than 60 µM abolished the formation of nuclei and mitotic waves.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the data in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Concentrations of importazole higher than 60 µM abolished the formation of nuclei and mitotic waves.
source: Mitotic waves were still observed with similar speeds for lower concentrations of importazole, while concentrations higher than 60 µM abolished the formation of nuclei and mitotic waves.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the data in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Increasing inhibition of nuclear import leads to smaller nuclei with dimmer levels of GFP-NLS.
source: Increasing inhibition of nuclear import was also found to lead to smaller nuclei with dimmer levels of GFP-NLS (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2G.

claim: When nuclei became very small (for 40 µM importazole), it took long for the extract to start cycling and mitotic waves were lost.
source: When nuclei became very small (i.e. for 40 µM importazole), it took long for the extract to start cycling and mitotic waves were lost (Figure 2F, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—video 2.

claim: Increasing concentrations of STLC gradually increased the average cell cycle period.
source: We found that increasing concentrations of STLC gradually increased the average cell cycle period (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nuclei no longer formed and mitotic waves were no longer observed when STLC was present in concentrations of approximately 40 µM.
source: Here too, nuclei no longer formed and mitotic waves were no longer observed when STLC was present in too high concentrations (approx. 40 µM STLC).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nuclear import processes are important in organizing mitotic waves.
source: Overall, these findings confirm that nuclear import processes are important in organizing mitotic waves.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings with importazole and STLC.

claim: Nuclear import processes ensure that nuclei are able to introduce sufficient spatial heterogeneity in cell cycle period to generate clear mitotic waves.
source: They ensure that nuclei are able to introduce sufficient spatial heterogeneity in cell cycle period to generate clear mitotic waves.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Brighter nuclei serve as pacemakers.
source: Based on our experimental observation showing that brighter nuclei serve as pacemakers, we set out to develop a theoretical model that describes how GFP-NLS and other proteins can be spatially redistributed by nuclei.
evidence: This is an experimental observation that motivates the theoretical model.

claim: The system toggles between interphase and mitosis with a fixed period in the computational model.
source: The system toggles between interphase and mitosis with a fixed period.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model shown in Figure 3A.

claim: During interphase, nuclei form and nuclear proteins are actively imported into the nucleus.
source: During interphase, nuclei form and nuclear proteins (such as GFP-NLS) are actively imported into the nucleus.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model shown in Figure 3A.

claim: During mitosis, the nuclear envelope breaks down and proteins are free to diffuse away.
source: During mitosis, the nuclear envelope breaks down and proteins are free to diffuse away.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model shown in Figure 3A.

claim: APC/C is mostly localized in the nucleus.
source: For example, it is known that APC/C is mostly localized in the nucleus, and Wee1 and Cdc25 are actively transported between cytoplasm and nucleus during the cell cycle (Baldin and Ducommun, 1995; Arnold et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baldin and Ducommun, 1995 and Arnold et al., 2015.

claim: Wee1 and Cdc25 are actively transported between cytoplasm and nucleus during the cell cycle.
source: For example, it is known that APC/C is mostly localized in the nucleus, and Wee1 and Cdc25 are actively transported between cytoplasm and nucleus during the cell cycle (Baldin and Ducommun, 1995; Arnold et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baldin and Ducommun, 1995 and Arnold et al., 2015.

claim: Relocalization of cell cycle regulators can locally change the cell cycle oscillation frequency.
source: Such relocalization of cell cycle regulators can locally change the cell cycle oscillation frequency.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the known behavior of cell cycle regulators.

claim: Increasing activity of Wee1 and APC/C tend to increase the cell cycle oscillation period.
source: For example, while increasing activity of Wee1 and APC/C tend to increase the cell cycle oscillation period, increasing Cdc25 activity leads to faster oscillations (Novak and Tyson, 1993; Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Novak and Tyson, 1993 and Tsai et al., 2014.

claim: Increasing Cdc25 activity leads to faster oscillations.
source: For example, while increasing activity of Wee1 and APC/C tend to increase the cell cycle oscillation period, increasing Cdc25 activity leads to faster oscillations (Novak and Tyson, 1993; Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Novak and Tyson, 1993 and Tsai et al., 2014.

claim: The overall effect of increasing nuclear import is to decrease the cell cycle period.
source: Our experiments thus suggest that the overall effect of increasing nuclear import is to decrease the cell cycle period.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: The distance between neighboring nuclei is typically around 150 µm.
source: From the experimental data, we calculated how far different nuclei are separated from each other, finding that the distance between neighboring nuclei is typically around 150 µm (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–I.

claim: The internuclear distance is consistent with the typical size of a nuclear domain in Xenopus cell-free extract.
source: Note that this distance is consistent with the typical size of a nuclear domain in Xenopus cell-free extract as mentioned before.
evidence: This is a comparison of the experimental observation with known literature values.

claim: The internuclear distance is consistent with the size of the recently characterized cell-like compartments that self-organize from homogenized interphase egg cytoplasm.
source: Moreover, the internuclear distance is also consistent with the size of the recently characterized cell-like compartments that self-organize from homogenized interphase egg cytoplasm (Cheng and Ferrell, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cheng and Ferrell, 2019.

claim: The build-up of regulators at the boundary is mainly attributed to the fact that nuclei in the interior of the domain compete with neighboring nuclei to attract the available proteins, while nuclei close to the boundary only have one such 'competitor'.
source: The build-up of regulators at the boundary is mainly attributed to the fact that nuclei in the interior of the domain compete with neighboring nuclei to attract the available proteins, while nuclei close to the boundary only have one such 'competitor'.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the computational modeling results.

claim: For decreasing numbers of nuclei, the build-up of regulators at the boundary gradually decreases.
source: Figure 3D shows that for decreasing numbers of nuclei (nine in green, five in orange, and three in red), the build-up of regulators at the boundary gradually decreases.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 3D.

claim: When only having three nuclei in the system, the central nucleus is found to be dominant and the boundary effect is completely lost.
source: When only having three nuclei in the system (red), the central nucleus is found to be dominant and the boundary effect is completely lost.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The extent to which regulators build up close to the boundary depends on the model parameters and on the exact nuclear distribution.
source: Although the extent to which regulators build up close to the boundary also depends on the model parameters and on the exact nuclear distribution (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4), it was found to be a robust phenomenon.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in multiple supplementary figures.

claim: Randomly removing a few nuclei within the domain could abolish the build-up of regulators at the boundary.
source: Interestingly, however, randomly removing a few nuclei within the domain could abolish the build-up of regulators at the boundary. Instead, proteins build up close to the nuclei adjacent to the gaps (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Nuclear cell cycle regulators build up at the edges of the domain in two-dimensional simulations.
source: Similarly as in the one-dimensional case, we observe that nuclear cell cycle regulators build up at the edges of the domain.
evidence: This is a result from the two-dimensional computational model shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The build-up of regulators at the boundary became more pronounced as the width of the domain increased in two-dimensional simulations.
source: This effect was particularly strong along the longest side of the rectangle, and strikingly, it became more pronounced as the width of the domain increased (see Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a result from the two-dimensional computational model shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: A spatial heterogeneity in the concentration of cell cycle regulators leads to a corresponding spatial frequency profile.
source: In this way a spatial heterogeneity in the concentration of cell cycle regulators leads to a corresponding spatial frequency profile.
evidence: This is a description of the expanded computational model.

claim: Spatial heterogeneities in the cell cycle period create multiple waves that propagate into the surrounding medium and compete with each other until the pacemaker with the highest frequency ultimately entrains the whole system.
source: In general, one expects that such spatial heterogeneities in the cell cycle period create multiple waves. These waves typically propagate into the surrounding medium and compete with each other until the pacemaker with the highest frequency ultimately entrains the whole system (Kuramoto, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuramoto, 1984.

claim: On average cell cycle regulators build up close to the boundary in simulations with 20 equidistantly distributed nuclei.
source: Figure 4A,D shows that on average cell cycle regulators build up close to the boundary, similarly as in Figure 3C.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 4A,D.

claim: The build-up of regulators at the boundary leads to a decreased cell cycle period at the boundary.
source: In the current model, however, this build-up of regulators also leads to a decreased cell cycle period at the boundary.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model.

claim: For moderate increases in nuclear import strength, a boundary-driven wave and a wave coming from the interior of the domain coexist.
source: For moderate increases in nuclear import strength, two waves compete with one another. A boundary-driven wave and a wave coming from the interior of the domain coexist (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Further increasing the nuclear import strength, waves no longer emerge from the boundary and are entirely controlled by the central region of 'bright' nuclei.
source: Further increasing the nuclear import strength, waves no longer emerged from the boundary and were entirely controlled by the central region of "bright" nuclei (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Removing a nucleus from the center of the domain leads to an increased concentration of regulators close to the central gap.
source: Figure 4E indeed illustrates that there is an increased concentration of regulators close to the central gap, but a build-up of regulators close to the boundary also persisted, such that two competing waves were found.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Removing three nuclei from the center causes the central pacemaker region to send out a wave that controls the whole domain.
source: We then removed two more nuclei from the center (Figure 4F), which caused the central pacemaker region to send out a wave that controlled the whole domain.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The fact that increasing nuclear import strengths and the absence of nuclei within a nuclear pattern both lead to the creation of waves from a nearby location is consistent with the experimental observations.
source: The fact that increasing nuclear import strengths and the absence of nuclei within a nuclear pattern both lead to the creation of waves from a nearby location is consistent with the experimental observations reported in Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a comparison of modeling results with experimental observations.

claim: A gradual transition from boundary-driven dynamics to internal pacemaker-driven dynamics was found in simulations continuously changing the relative strength of both pacemaker regions.
source: We found a gradual transition from boundary-driven dynamics to internal pacemaker-driven dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Similar results were found by using the FitzHugh-Nagumo oscillator model.
source: Similar results were found by using the FitzHugh-Nagumo oscillator model, a general model for relaxation-type oscillatory systems (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Even more sinusoidal oscillations preserved boundary-driven waves.
source: Moreover, we found that even more sinusoidal oscillations preserved boundary-driven waves (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The generation of boundary-driven waves is largely independent of the type of oscillations, as long as the oscillation period is decreased close to the boundary.
source: This suggests that the generation of boundary-driven waves is largely independent of the type of oscillations, as long as the oscillation period is decreased close to the boundary.
evidence: This is an inference from the computational modeling results.

claim: Pacemaker-driven traveling waves form thanks to spatial heterogeneities that locally increase the oscillation frequency.
source: Pacemaker-driven traveling waves, also often referred to as target patterns, have been widely studied and they form thanks to spatial heterogeneities that locally increase the oscillation frequency.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about pacemaker waves.

claim: Pacemaker waves were initially observed in chemical reaction-diffusion systems where heterogeneities were introduced as dust particles that locally modified the properties of the medium.
source: The majority of such pacemaker waves were initially observed in chemical reaction-diffusion systems where heterogeneities were introduced as dust particles that locally modified the properties of the medium (Zaikin and Zhabotinsky, 1970; Zhabotinsky and Zaikin, 1973; Tyson and Fife, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zaikin and Zhabotinsky, 1970; Zhabotinsky and Zaikin, 1973; and Tyson and Fife, 1980.

claim: Pacemakers propagate into the surrounding medium and compete with each other until the pacemaker with the highest frequency ultimately entrains the whole system.
source: In general, they propagate into the surrounding medium and compete with each other until the pacemaker with the highest frequency ultimately entrains the whole system (Kuramoto, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuramoto, 1984.

claim: The transition region where boundary-driven waves and internal pacemaker-driven waves coexist shrinks with increasingly longer transient times.
source: However, simulating the system for increasingly longer transient times, we find that the transition region where boundary-driven waves and internal pacemaker-driven waves coexist shrinks, suggesting that after infinitely long transients one pacemaker indeed controls the whole domain.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model.

claim: The early embryonic cell cycle oscillations only persist for about 13 cycles.
source: Such infinite transient times are, however, less biologically relevant as the early embryonic cell cycle oscillations only persist for about 13 cycles (Box 2).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the biological system.

claim: One would expect to observe the full range of transient pacemaker dynamics in actual biological systems.
source: Therefore, one would expect to observe the full range of transient pacemaker dynamics in actual biological systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limited number of cell cycles in the biological system.

claim: Wider systems lead to higher concentrations of cell cycle regulators at the boundary.
source: First, wider systems lead to higher concentrations of cell cycle regulators at the boundary.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model.

claim: A local decrease of the cell cycle period leads to boundary-driven mitotic waves.
source: Such a local decrease of the cell cycle period leads to boundary-driven mitotic waves.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model.

claim: Systems with intermediate width allow both internally- and boundary-driven pacemakers.
source: Second, systems with intermediate width allow both internally- and boundary-driven pacemakers.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model.

claim: Sparsely distributed nuclei favor internal pacemakers.
source: Third, sparsely distributed nuclei favor internal pacemakers.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model.

claim: The thinnest tube shows mitotic waves coordinated by internal pacemakers.
source: While the thinnest tube shows mitotic waves coordinated by internal pacemakers, mitotic waves are boundary-driven over the whole domain in the thickest tube.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Video 2.

claim: Mitotic waves are boundary-driven over the whole domain in the thickest tube.
source: While the thinnest tube shows mitotic waves coordinated by internal pacemakers, mitotic waves are boundary-driven over the whole domain in the thickest tube.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Video 2.

claim: In tubes of intermediate width (200 and 300 µm), boundary-driven waves coexist with mitotic waves that are driven by internal pacemakers.
source: Furthermore, Video 2 illustrates that in tubes of intermediate width (200 and 300 µm), boundary-driven waves coexist with mitotic waves that are driven by internal pacemakers.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Video 2.

claim: The thinnest tubes have the lowest probability of finding boundary-driven mitotic waves.
source: While the thinnest tubes have the lowest probability of finding boundary-driven mitotic waves, all of the experiments with the thickest 560 µm tubes showed boundary-driven waves (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: All of the experiments with the thickest 560 µm tubes showed boundary-driven waves.
source: While the thinnest tubes have the lowest probability of finding boundary-driven mitotic waves, all of the experiments with the thickest 560 µm tubes showed boundary-driven waves (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The fraction of experiments with boundary-driven wave dynamics increased smoothly with the tube width.
source: The fraction of experiments with boundary-driven wave dynamics increased smoothly with the tube width.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the data in Figure 5A.

claim: Using a lower concentration of added sperm nuclei (≈ 60 nuclei/µl) strongly decreased the probability for mitotic waves to originate from the boundary.
source: Next, we repeated the experiments using a lower concentration of added sperm nuclei (≈ 60 nuclei/µl). This strongly decreased the probability for mitotic waves to originate from the boundary (see Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The regularity of the nuclear pattern was disrupted due to the decreased amount of nuclei.
source: We noticed that the regularity of the nuclear pattern was disrupted due to the decreased amount of nuclei.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The absence of neighboring nuclei was found to strengthen nearby pacemaker regions and decreased the likelihood of having pacemaker regions at the boundary.
source: Consistent with our third theoretical prediction, the absence of neighboring nuclei was found to strengthen nearby pacemaker regions and decreased the likelihood of having pacemaker regions at the boundary (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: All experiments with droplets of cycling cell-free extracts on Teflon-coated glass slides showed that mitosis was coordinated via mitotic waves that originate at the boundary.
source: Therefore, we carried out experiments with droplets of cycling cell-free extracts on Teflon-coated glass slides, providing a thin structure, yet wide in diameter (≈ 1 mm). All such experiments showed that mitosis was coordinated via mitotic waves that originate at the boundary, consistent with the theoretical predictions (see Video 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Video 2.

claim: There is a higher build-up of GFP-NLS intensity towards the boundaries in wider tubes.
source: This analysis confirmed that there is a higher build-up of GFP-NLS intensity towards the boundaries in wider tubes (see Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Increasing the spatial dimensions of the system leads to a higher probability of observing mitotic waves that originate at the boundary of the system.
source: Our findings illustrate that the spatial environment has a strong influence on how biological processes self-organize. In particular, increasing the spatial dimensions of the system leads to a higher probability of observing mitotic waves that originate at the boundary of the system.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Cytoplasmic volume determines the spindle size in cell-free frog extracts.
source: For example, using cell-free frog extracts, cytoplasmic volume was demonstrated to determine the spindle size (Good et al., 2013; Hazel et al., 2013) and the size of the nucleus (Hara and Merten, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Good et al., 2013 and Hazel et al., 2013.

claim: Cytoplasmic volume determines the size of the nucleus in cell-free frog extracts.
source: For example, using cell-free frog extracts, cytoplasmic volume was demonstrated to determine the spindle size (Good et al., 2013; Hazel et al., 2013) and the size of the nucleus (Hara and Merten, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hara and Merten, 2015.

claim: System boundaries affect the dynamics of traveling waves.
source: System boundaries (Kopell et al., 1991; Haim et al., 1996; Rabinovitch et al., 2001; McNamara et al., 2016; Bernitt et al., 2017) and system geometry (Wettmann et al., 2018) have been shown to affect the dynamics of traveling waves.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: System geometry affects the dynamics of traveling waves.
source: System boundaries (Kopell et al., 1991; Haim et al., 1996; Rabinovitch et al., 2001; McNamara et al., 2016; Bernitt et al., 2017) and system geometry (Wettmann et al., 2018) have been shown to affect the dynamics of traveling waves.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wettmann et al., 2018.

claim: In Dictyostelium discoideum, waves appear spontaneously in areas of higher cell density with the oscillation frequency of these centers depending on their density.
source: Waves appear spontaneously in areas of higher cell density with the oscillation frequency of these centers depending on their density (Vidal-Henriquez and Gholami, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vidal-Henriquez and Gholami, 2019.

claim: In the presence of advection, a boundary-induced instability was found to periodically excite a cAMP wave near the boundary in Dictyostelium discoideum.
source: In the presence of advection, a boundary-induced instability was found to periodically excite a cAMP wave near the boundary (Vidal-Henriquez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vidal-Henriquez et al., 2017.

claim: Min-protein wave patterns help select the site of cell division in Escherichia coli.
source: Another well-characterized model organism is the bacterium Escherichia coli, where Min-protein wave patterns help select the site of cell division (Hu and Lutkenhaus, 1999; Raskin and de Boer, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu and Lutkenhaus, 1999 and Raskin and de Boer, 1999.

claim: Wave patterns and the location of cell division strongly depend on the system size and geometry in Escherichia coli.
source: Wave patterns and the location of cell division have been shown to strongly depend on the system size and geometry, both in vivo by deforming cell shape (Männik et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2015; Wettmann et al., 2018) and in vitro by reconstituting Min oscillations in open and enclosed compartments (Zieske and Schwille, 2014; Zieske et al., 2016; Caspi and Dekker, 2016; Wettmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: As thin compartments were gradually increased in length, multiple regions of oscillations were observed in Min protein systems.
source: As thin compartments were gradually increased in length, multiple regions of oscillations were observed (Zieske and Schwille, 2014; Zieske et al., 2016; Caspi and Dekker, 2016; Wettmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the Min system, wave patterns are mainly controlled by the spatial dimensions and geometry.
source: While there are similarities with our findings in the Xenopus cell-free extracts, one important difference is that the wave patterns in the Min system are mainly controlled by the spatial dimensions and geometry.
evidence: This is a comparison with the Min system.

claim: In the Xenopus cell-free extracts, the influence of the spatial dimensions are, at least partially, mediated by the nuclei within the oscillatory medium that serve as pacemakers.
source: In contrast, in our findings the influence of the spatial dimensions are, at least partially, mediated by the nuclei within the oscillatory medium that serve as pacemakers.
evidence: This is a summary of the key difference between the current findings and the Min system.

claim: Nuclei act as pacemakers generating the mitotic waves in Xenopus cell-free extracts.
source: We have demonstrated that nuclei act as pacemakers generating the mitotic waves in Xenopus cell-free extracts.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: A nucleus becomes a pacemaker by its ability to import factors into the nucleus and concentrate cell cycle regulators.
source: A nucleus becomes a pacemaker by its ability to import factors into the nucleus and, presumably, concentrate cell cycle regulators.
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanism by which nuclei act as pacemakers.

claim: The distribution of cell cycle regulators depends on the nuclear positioning and spatial dimensions of the system.
source: We built a generic computational model, which showed that the distribution of cell cycle regulators also depends on the nuclear positioning and spatial dimensions of the system.
evidence: This is a summary of the computational modeling results.

claim: In cell-free extracts with only few nuclei, mitotic waves originated at those nuclei and spread through the parts of the extract devoid of nuclei.
source: In cell-free extracts with only few nuclei, we found that mitotic waves originated at those nuclei and spread through the parts of the extract devoid of nuclei.
evidence: This is a summary of an experimental finding.

claim: In the absence of any nuclei in the system, no mitotic waves were observed.
source: In the absence of any nuclei in the system, no mitotic waves were observed.
evidence: This is a summary of an experimental finding.

claim: Decreasing the nuclear import strength avoided the formation of mitotic waves.
source: Decreasing the nuclear import strength similarly avoided the formation of mitotic waves.
evidence: This is a summary of an experimental finding.

claim: Thicker tubes have a larger tendency to concentrate cell cycle regulators at the boundaries, leading to mitotic waves originating at the outer edges of the tubes.
source: Finally, we changed the spatial dimensions of the system, and found that thicker tubes have a larger tendency to concentrate cell cycle regulators at the boundaries, leading to mitotic waves originating at the outer edges of the tubes.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: One advantage to having the nucleus control the timing of mitosis is that it allows the cell to ensure that DNA replication has completed before initiating mitosis.
source: One advantage to having the nucleus control the timing of mitosis is that it allows the cell to ensure that DNA replication has completed before initiating mitosis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: DNA checkpoints are largely silenced in the early Xenopus embryo.
source: While DNA checkpoints are largely silenced in the early Xenopus embryo (Newport and Dasso, 1989), in Drosophila DNA content is known to activate the DNA-replication checkpoint and alter the cell cycle period (Farrell and O'Farrell, 2014; Deneke et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Newport and Dasso, 1989.

claim: In Drosophila DNA content is known to activate the DNA-replication checkpoint and alter the cell cycle period.
source: While DNA checkpoints are largely silenced in the early Xenopus embryo (Newport and Dasso, 1989), in Drosophila DNA content is known to activate the DNA-replication checkpoint and alter the cell cycle period (Farrell and O'Farrell, 2014; Deneke et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Farrell and O'Farrell, 2014 and Deneke et al., 2016.

claim: A failure in the correct regulation of mitosis is associated with polyploidy, which plays a key role in nonmalignant physiological and pathological processes.
source: A failure in the correct regulation of mitosis is associated with polyploidy, which plays a key role in nonmalignant physiological and pathological processes (Fox and Duronio, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fox and Duronio, 2013.

claim: In the absence of a proper pacemaker, or if the pacemaker were to be located elsewhere, linking DNA replication to mitosis would be more complicated and, perhaps, more prone to error.
source: In the absence of a proper pacemaker, or if the pacemaker were to be located elsewhere, linking DNA replication to mitosis would be more complicated and, perhaps, more prone to error.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential consequences.

claim: Previous studies have pointed to the critical role of the nucleus in spatial redistributing cell cycle regulators.
source: Previous studies have pointed to the critical role of the nucleus in spatial redistributing cell cycle regulators (Gavet and Pines, 2010; Santos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gavet and Pines, 2010 and Santos et al., 2012.

claim: The nuclear import of Cyclin B has been shown to lead to spatial positive feedback, ensuring a robust and irreversible mitotic entry.
source: In particular, the nuclear import of Cyclin B has been shown to lead to spatial positive feedback, ensuring a robust and irreversible mitotic entry (Santos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Santos et al., 2012.

claim: Nuclei have been found to be crucial in ensuring cell cycle oscillations in the Drosophila embryo.
source: Nuclei have also been found to be crucial in ensuring cell cycle oscillations in the Drosophila embryo (Huang and Raff, 1999; Deneke et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang and Raff, 1999 and Deneke et al., 2019.

claim: Although previous reports have suggested that centrosomes serve as pacemakers, the current study found that they are dispensable.
source: Interestingly, although previous reports have suggested that centrosomes serve as pacemakers (Chang and Ferrell, 2013; Ishihara et al., 2014), we found that they are dispensable.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study that contradicts previous suggestions.

claim: After treating extracts with purified DNA, which lacks centrosomes, mitotic waves were still observed.
source: After treating extracts with purified DNA, which lacks centrosomes, we still observed mitotic waves.
evidence: This is an experimental finding that supports the claim that centrosomes are dispensable.

claim: Nuclei self-organize in regular spatial patterns within a tube of Xenopus cell-free extract.
source: We also found that the interaction of multiple nuclei in a shared cytoplasm can lead to unexpected behavior. Nuclei self-organize in regular spatial patterns within a tube of Xenopus cell-free extract.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The measured regular spacing between neighboring nuclei was found to be approximately 150 µm, which coincides with the nuclear subdomain of the cytoplasm in which spatial constraints show an effect on nuclear growth.
source: The measured regular spacing between neighboring nuclei was found to be approximately 150 µm, which coincides with the nuclear subdomain of the cytoplasm in which spatial constraints show an effect on nuclear growth as studied in syncytial muscle fibers (Landing et al., 1974), Drosophila embryos (Telley et al., 2012), and cell-free frog extracts (Hara and Merten, 2015).
evidence: This is an experimental observation that is consistent with known literature values.

claim: The internuclear distance is consistent with the size of cell-like compartments that spontaneously form in homogenized interphase cell-free frog extracts.
source: It is also consistent with the size of cell-like compartments that spontaneously form in homogenized interphase cell-free frog extracts (Cheng and Ferrell, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cheng and Ferrell, 2019.

claim: Regularity in the nuclear distribution led to a build-up of cell cycle regulators towards the boundary of the system, such that the collective behavior of many nuclei creates a pacemaker region at the boundary of the oscillatory medium.
source: We found that such regularity in the nuclear distribution led to a build-up of cell cycle regulators towards the boundary of the system, such that the collective behavior of many nuclei creates a pacemaker region at the boundary of the oscillatory medium.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from both modeling and experiments.

claim: The boundary effect was stronger with increasing widths of the tubes, in the presence of more extended regular nuclear patterns.
source: This boundary effect was stronger with increasing widths of the tubes, in the presence of more extended regular nuclear patterns.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: More boundary-driven waves were consistently observed in wider tubes.
source: We consistently observed more boundary-driven waves in such wider tubes.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Mitotic waves in the early Drosophila embryo also often originate at the boundary.
source: Mitotic waves in the early Drosophila embryo also often originate at the boundary (Foe and Alberts, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Foe and Alberts, 1983.

claim: During nuclear cycles 10–13 in the syncytial blastoderm of early Drosophila embryos, nuclei enter (and exit) mitosis in waves that originate from the opposite anterior and posterior poles of the embryo and terminate in its mid-region.
source: During nuclear cycles 10–13 in the syncytial blastoderm of these early embryos, nuclei enter (and exit) mitosis in waves that originate from the opposite anterior and posterior poles of the embryo and terminate in its mid-region.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about Drosophila embryos.

claim: Mitotic waves are associated to trigger waves in the Xenopus embryo.
source: While mitotic waves are associated to so-called trigger waves in the Xenopus embryo (Chang and Ferrell, 2013; Gelens et al., 2014), they have been shown to be so-called sweep waves in the Drosophila embryo (Vergassola et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chang and Ferrell, 2013 and Gelens et al., 2014.

claim: Mitotic waves have been shown to be sweep waves in the Drosophila embryo.
source: While mitotic waves are associated to so-called trigger waves in the Xenopus embryo (Chang and Ferrell, 2013; Gelens et al., 2014), they have been shown to be so-called sweep waves in the Drosophila embryo (Vergassola et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vergassola et al., 2018.

claim: By computational modeling, sweep waves are able to generate boundary-driven waves in a syncytium.
source: We find, by computational modeling, that sweep waves are also able to generate boundary-driven waves in a syncytium, and that they propagate faster than trigger waves as predicted by Vergassola et al. (2018); Figure 4—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sweep waves propagate faster than trigger waves.
source: We find, by computational modeling, that sweep waves are also able to generate boundary-driven waves in a syncytium, and that they propagate faster than trigger waves as predicted by Vergassola et al. (2018); Figure 4—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model and is consistent with predictions by Vergassola et al., 2018.

claim: The internuclear distance of the simulations is significantly larger than the one observed in the more crowded Drosophila embryo.
source: However, the internuclear distance of our simulations is significantly larger than the one observed in the more crowded Drosophila embryo, so it remains unclear whether our results can directly extend to that system.
evidence: This is a limitation of the model when comparing to Drosophila embryos.

claim: The work is expected to be relevant for all coenocytes, where waves of mitosis have also been observed.
source: Despite the limitations of the model, our work is expected to be relevant for all coenocytes (Ondracka et al., 2018), where waves of mitosis have also been observed (Sears, 1967; Brown et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ondracka et al., 2018; Sears, 1967; and Brown et al., 2003.

claim: Nuclei are a natural choice of pacemaker for mitotic waves because they allow for a natural way to link one biological process, DNA replication, with another, mitosis.
source: Nuclei are a natural choice of pacemaker for mitotic waves because they allow for a natural way to link one biological process, DNA replication, with another, mitosis.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: Traveling waves have been found to propagate apoptosis.
source: Traveling waves have, for example, also been found to propagate apoptosis (Cheng and Ferrell, 2018), action potentials (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952), and calcium signals (Stricker, 1999) over large distances.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cheng and Ferrell, 2018.

claim: Traveling waves have been found to propagate action potentials.
source: Traveling waves have, for example, also been found to propagate apoptosis (Cheng and Ferrell, 2018), action potentials (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952), and calcium signals (Stricker, 1999) over large distances.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952.

claim: Traveling waves have been found to propagate calcium signals.
source: Traveling waves have, for example, also been found to propagate apoptosis (Cheng and Ferrell, 2018), action potentials (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952), and calcium signals (Stricker, 1999) over large distances.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stricker, 1999.

claim: In apoptosis systems, defective mitochondria serve as the initial trigger to locally activate a wave.
source: In these systems, defective mitochondria, signals from neighboring neurons, or fertilization serve as the initial trigger to locally activate a wave.
evidence: This is stated as an example of how waves are initiated in other biological systems.

claim: In neuronal systems, signals from neighboring neurons serve as the initial trigger to locally activate a wave.
source: In these systems, defective mitochondria, signals from neighboring neurons, or fertilization serve as the initial trigger to locally activate a wave.
evidence: This is stated as an example of how waves are initiated in other biological systems.

claim: In calcium signaling systems, fertilization serves as the initial trigger to locally activate a wave.
source: In these systems, defective mitochondria, signals from neighboring neurons, or fertilization serve as the initial trigger to locally activate a wave.
evidence: This is stated as an example of how waves are initiated in other biological systems.
